## Learning objectives

- distinguish a persistence migration from a query projection
- design a document around an aggregate and its access patterns
- use `MongoRepository`, embedded documents, and unique indexes
- reason about document atomicity and schema evolution
- compare the MongoDB aggregate with the former SQL mapping

## Prerequisite: direct document manipulation

[Tutorial 11b](../11b-mongodb-with-mongosh/slides.qmd) introduces BSON,
embedded documents, update operators, indexes, query plans, aggregation, and
single-document atomicity directly in `mongosh`.

This module now applies those mechanics to production code: Spring Data maps
the domain aggregate, unique indexes enforce business identities, and a MongoDB
transaction commits the aggregate together with its outbox intent.

## Persistence migration, not a projection

`InsuranceOffer` is business state: it owns the `PROPOSED → ACCEPTED`
invariant and is the source of truth for accepting complementary insurance.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  Auction[AuctionWon v1] --> Insurance[insuranceService]
  Insurance --> Offer[(insurance.insurance_offers)]
  UI -->|GET / POST accept| Insurance
```

Changing its store from H2/PostgreSQL to MongoDB changes persistence. It does
not make the aggregate derived or safely disposable.

## Access patterns drive the document

The service needs to find an offer by `rentalId`, reject a repeated
`AuctionWon` by `eventId`, and update status plus acceptance metadata together.

```json
{
  "rental_id": "RENT-42",
  "event_id": "auction-event-uuid",
  "vehicle": { "car_id": 42, "plate_number": "EDU-042", "brand": "Tesla", "model": "Model 3" },
  "rental_daily_price": 62,
  "daily_premium": 7,
  "status": "PROPOSED"
}
```

## Embedding and atomicity

Vehicle facts are embedded because they are read with the offer and do not
have an independent lifecycle inside this service. A single-document update
atomically changes status, `accepted_event_id`, `accepted_at`, and `updated_at`.

Atomicity normally stops at one document. Here MongoDB runs as a replica set,
so one transaction commits the aggregate and an `insurance_outbox` document.
A relay publishes that durable intent to Redis later. Stable event identifiers
make the relay's at-least-once delivery safe.

## Repository and indexes

```java
public interface InsuranceOfferRepository
    extends MongoRepository<InsuranceOffer, String> {
  Optional<InsuranceOffer> findByRentalId(String rentalId);
  Optional<InsuranceOffer> findByEventId(String eventId);
}
```

- unique `event_id`: one effect per source event;
- unique `rental_id`: one current offer per rental;
- `_id`: MongoDB identity, not the business lookup key.

Indexes accelerate reads but add storage and write work. Auto-creation is
useful for this lab; managed migrations are preferable in production.

## Schema evolution

- New optional fields can be read with defaults.
- Renames require dual-read/migration periods.
- New required invariants require validation and backfill.
- Event schema version and document schema evolution are separate concerns.

Rolling deployments must tolerate both old and new document shapes.

## SQL versus document storage

| Concern | Former relational mapping | MongoDB aggregate |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregate load | row plus joins as model grows | one document |
| Atomic boundary | transaction across rows | one document by default |
| Constraints | relational constraints | indexes + application invariants |
| Evolution | explicit DDL migration | tolerant reads + backfill |
| Ad hoc relations | strong | deliberately limited |

MongoDB fits this bounded aggregate; it is not automatically better for every query.

## Architecture checkpoint

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  Redis[[Redis ready/processing Lists]] --> Consumer[Idempotent insurance consumer]
  Consumer -->|event_id unique| Aggregate[(insurance_offers)]
  Aggregate --> API[Insurance REST API]
  Consumer -->|same Mongo transaction| Outbox[(insurance_outbox)]
  Outbox --> Relay[Retrying outbox relay]
  Relay --> Published[[events:simple:published]]
```
